Eﬀect of pH, substrate loading, oxygen, and methanogens inhibitors on
volatile fatty acid (VFA) production from citrus waste by anaerobic
digestion
Bahriye Eryildiza,b, Lukitawesab,⁎, Mohammad J. Taherzadehb
a Istanbul Technical University, Environmental Engineering Department, Maslak, 34469 Istanbul, Turkey
b Swedish Centre for Resource Recovery, University of Borås, SE 501-90 Borås, Sweden
G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Volatile fatty acids
Inoculum to substrate ratio
2-bromoethanesulfonate (BES)
Oxygen
Anaerobic digestion, citrus waste
A B S T R A C T
Citrus waste from e.g., juice production is a potential substrate for anaerobic digestion (AD). However, due to the
toxic citrus peel oil content, citrus waste has several challenges in biogas production. Hence, volatile fatty acids
(VFAs) are very interesting intermediate products of AD. This paper was aimed to investigate VFA production
from citrus wastes by boosting its production and inhibiting methane formation. Therefore, the eﬀects of in-
oculum to substrate ratio (ISR), O2 presence, pH, and inhibitor for methanogens, in VFA production from citrus
waste through acidiﬁcation process were studied. The addition of 2 g/L methanogens inhibitor and the presence
of O2 in the reactors were able to reduce methane production. The highest yield of VFA (0.793 g VFA/g VSadded)
was achieved at controlled pH at 6 and low substrate loading (ISR 1:1). Acetic acid (32%), caproic acid (21%),
and butyric acid (15%) dominate the VFA composition in this condition.
1. Introduction
Citrus is one of the most abundant genus of fruits in the world.
According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United
Nations (FAO), global citrus production increased by 20.6% from 2006
to 2016, to 132.4 million tones (FAO, 2017). Approximately, 98% of
the industrialized citrus harvest consists of orange, mandarin, grape-
fruit, and lemon. Citrus fruits are mainly processed to obtain fruit juice.
They are also used in many ﬁelds such as the canning industry, che-
mical industry, food industry, cosmetics, and pharmaceutical industries

(Marín et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2017). Approximately, 40–60% of citrus
production is used in fruit juice production, and as a result of this
process, 50–60% of the citrus mass ends up in waste streams
(Wikandari et al., 2014a). Dumping and landﬁlling for citrus waste
causes several environmental challenges such as unpleasant odor and
leachates. This wastes attracts ﬂies and rats due to its low pH, high
water content, and high organic matter content, and high biodegrad-
ability (Ruiz and Flotats, 2014; Wikandari et al., 2014a). Therefore,
alternative methods to face these challenges have been investigated.
The high moisture content of citrus wastes is a limitation and make it
unsuitable for combustion and incineration. The possibility of energy
production by anaerobic digestion which is more environmentally
friendly than other alternatives (Xu et al., 2018).
Anaerobic digestion is a biological process that can be used for
treating organic wastes. The digestion performance (e.g. biogas pro-
duction, organic reduction, inhibition characteristics, and process sta-
bility) is highly dependent on the feedstock’s characteristics (Li et al.,
2017). The anaerobic process consists of four main stages: hydrolysis,
acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis (Wainaina et al.,
2019). In the ﬁrst phase of the anaerobic digestion process, i.e. hy-
drolysis, complex organic polymers are broken down into simple so-
luble monomers by means of extracellular enzymes formed by hydro-
lytic
microorganisms
(Debruyn
and
Hilborn,
2007).
During
the
acidogenesis phase, products formed in the hydrolysis phase are con-
verted to volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and minor products such as hy-
drogen, carbon dioxide (CO2), and acetic acid by acidogenic bacteria. In
the acetogenesis phase, acetogenic bacteria further convert VFAs to
acetate, CO2, and/or hydrogen (Debruyn and Hilborn, 2007; Khan
et al., 2016). In the last phase, methanogenic microorganisms convert
products of acidogenesis and acetogenesis into carbon dioxide and
methane (Massé et al., 2011). However, citrus waste has been known as
a diﬃcult substrate for methane production due to the citrus peel oil
content which is toxic for the methanogens (Fuertes, 2015; Kurniawan
et al., 2018; Lukitawesa et al., 2018; Ruiz et al., 2016; Ruiz and Flotats,
2014; Ruiz and Flotats, 2016; Wikandari et al., 2014a; Wikandari et al.,
2015). Citrus peel oil contains the monoterpenes limonene (65–77%),
γ-terpinene (13–21%), α-pinene (1.5–3.0%), β-pinene (1.3–2.5%), β-
myrcene (1.5–2.5%). There are also alcohols citronellol, geraniol, and
linalool (combined total 1–1.5%) and smaller amounts of aldehydes,
esters, and phenols (Clarke, 2008) present in the peel oil.
Recent studies have shown that the anaerobic digestion (AD) pro-
cess could be designed to produce biogas as well as volatile fatty acids
(Wainaina et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2018). VFAs, which
are a product of the acidogenesis phase, consist mainly of acetic acid,
propionic acid, butyric acid, and valeric acid (Wainaina et al., 2019).
The operational parameters, substrate composition, available microbial
community, the process design, and type of reactor aﬀect the amount
and composition of VFAs produced (Li et al., 2013; Stein et al., 2017;
Wainaina et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014).
In order to produce VFAs, the methanogens that utilize VFAs should
be inhibited. Several studies have shown that 2-bromoethanesulfonate
(BES) has the ability to inhibit the activity of the methanogens
(Chidthaisong and Conrad, 2000; Zinder et al., 1984); having an op-
timum concentration of around 50 Mm for complete inhibition (Zinder
et al., 1984). Another study has reported that the addition of 1 µmol/
mL of BES could reduce 60% of methanogen activity, leading to an
increased acetate accumulation (Mohan et al., 2008). The previous
study had been investigating the eﬀect of diﬀerent factors such as O2
presence, inoculum to substrate ratio (ISR), BES, and pH towards VFA
production from food waste (Lukitawesa et al., 2020). There is a scarce
of study to investigate the eﬀect of those factors at the same time for
toxic feedstock, such as citrus waste.
In the form of VFA, acetic acid has the highest in the market size,
with 3,500,000 tons/year and price per ton 800 $. It is followed by
propionic acid with 180,000 tons/year and price per ton 1700 $.
Butyric acid and caproic acid have the smallest market size at are
30,000 tons/year and 25,000 tons/year, respectively. The price of tons
per ton is 2500 $ (Jankowska et al., 2017).
Volatile fatty acids (VFAs) are used in many ﬁelds such as bio-
plastics synthesis, biological nitrogen removal, and bioenergy produc-
tion, for example, as alternatives to traditional external carbon sources
in municipal wastewater treatment (Xie et al., 2014; Yin et al., 2016). In
addition, with an appropriate method, VFA can be converted to alco-
hols, biohydrogen, microalgal lipids, bioelectricity, aldehydes, ketones,
alkanes, polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA), a biopolymer used for biode-
gradable plastics production, and can also ﬁnd a direct usage as food
additives in the food and the pharmaceutical industries (Dahiya et al.,
2015; Khan et al., 2016; Trad et al., 2015; Wainaina et al., 2019).
The VFA production from citrus waste was previously reported in
two-stage anaerobic digestion with the highest yield of 0.125 g VFA/
g VSadded (Lukitawesa et al., 2018). The VFA concentration in a one-
stage reactor which digests citrus waste at organic loading rate 3 g VS/
L.d without pH control was around 6 g/L, which means the yield was
only 0.072 g VFA/g VSadded (Wikandari et al., 2014a). However, those
studies were mainly focused on producing methane instead of VFA.
There is no information on whether citrus peel oil can also inhibit the
other steps in anaerobic digestion i.e., hydrolysis and acidiﬁcation
process.
The objective of this study was to investigate the eﬀect of various
factors such as pH, BES, inoculum to substrate ratio, and oxygen on the
production of VFA from citrus waste under anaerobic conditions. This
study was divided into two cultures. In the ﬁrst culture, the eﬀect of
BES, oxygen, and inoculum to substrate ratio on the concentration,
yield, and composition of VFA produced from citrus waste was in-
vestigated. In the second culture, the eﬀect of pH and inoculum to
substrate ratio on VFA concentration, yield, and composition produced
from citrus waste was investigated. Besides, biogas production as a
byproduct and the compositions were investigated in both cultures.
2. Materials and method
2.1. Inoculum
Sludge used as inoculum was obtained from a digester treating food
waste sludge and operating at mesophilic conditions (Vatten and Miljö i
Väst AB, Varberg, Sweden). The inoculum was ﬁltered through a 2 mm
porosity sieve to remove unwanted particles, after which it was accli-
mated for ﬁve days in an incubator at 37 °C before use.
2.2. Substrate
Citrus wastes were taken from Brämhult juice AB (Borås, Sweden).
The characteristics of the citrus waste used in this culture are shown in

2.3. Eﬀect of initial O2 presence, the addition of inhibitor for methanogens,
and ISR on the production of VFAs
The anaerobic process was performed in order to examine the eﬀect
of diﬀerent inoculum-substrate ratios, the eﬀect of BES, and oxygen on
the VFA production. This culture was studied with 16 diﬀerent reactors
in 8 diﬀerent states (Table 1) in 120 mL of glass serum bottles as re-
actors with a working volume of 56 mL. The cultivations were con-
ducted in duplicate for 14 days. When the inoculum/substrate ratio was
1:1, each bioreactor contained 1 g volatile solids (VS) of inoculum and
1 g VS of ground citrus waste. However, when the inoculum/substrate
ratio is 1:3, each bioreactor contained 1 g VS of inoculum and 3 g VS of
ground citrus waste. In this stage, the cultures in all reactors were ad-
justed to pH 6, and there was no pH adjustment for 14 days. The re-
actors were then closed and incubated under anaerobic conditions at
37.5 °C with 100 rpm. Each reactor put on a shaker for 14 days.
2.4. Eﬀect of controlled pH conditions and ISR on the production of VFAs
The anaerobic digestion was performed in order to investigate the
eﬀect of diﬀerent inoculum-substrate ratios, and the eﬀect of pH on
VFA production. This culture setup was conducted with six diﬀerent
states (Table 2). In this cultivation, 2 L glass bottle bioreactors was used
as a batch digester with a total working volume of 1.5 L. Studies were
continued for 22 days. When the inoculum/substrate ratio was 1:1,
each bioreactor contained 25 g VS of free cells of inoculum and 25 g VS
of ground citrus waste. However, when the inoculum/substrate ratio
was 1:3, each bioreactor contained 25 g VS of free cells of inoculum and
75 g VS of ground citrus waste. In this cultivation, the experiment was
carried out at three diﬀerent pH of 4, 5, and 6. The pH was adjusted
every two days to maintain the desired pH values constant. The pH
adjustment was carried out by the addition of 2 M NaOH and/or 2 M
HCl. The digesters were incubated under the anaerobic condition at
37.5 °C with 100 rpm.
2.5. Analytical methods
The moisture content, total solid (TS), volatile solid (VS), and vo-
latile suspended solids (VSS) of substrates and inoculum were de-
termined according to biomass analytical procedures (APHA-AWWA-
WEF, 2005). Total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN) contents were measured
using the Kjeldahl method, and the protein content was estimated by
multiplying the TKN content with a factor of 6.25 (Nallathambi
Gunaseelan, 2009). Total carbon was obtained by correcting the total
dry weight carbon value for the ash content (Haug, 1993; Zhou et al.,
2015). Fat content was determined using the Soxhlet extraction pro-
cedure (Carpenter, 2010). The pH and oxidation-reduction potential
(ORP) were measured using pH- and ORP-meter (Mettler Toledo F20
FiveEasy, OH, USA) Samples from reactors were centrifuged (5 min at
20,000×g), and supernatants were collected for the analyses of VFAs.
VFAs were measured using high-performance liquid chromato-
graphy (HPLC, Waters 2695, Waters Corporation, Milford, MA, USA)
equipped with a biohydrogen-ion exchange column (Aminex HPX-87H,
Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) operating at 60 °C. For the detection of
VFAs, an UV absorbance detector (Walters 2487, Waters Corporation
Milford, MA, USA), operating at 210 nm wavelength was used in series
with a refractive index (RI) detector (Waters 2414, Waters Corporation
Milford, MA, USA) operating at 60 °C. Prior to analysis, samples were
ﬁrst centrifuged at 20,000×g for 10 min to exclude the natant from the
analysis. The supernatant was then ﬁltered using an HPLC certiﬁed
syringe ﬁlter (GHP Acrodisc 13 mm with 0.2 μm GHP membrane) to
remove remaining contaminant particles, which might hinder column
separation.
Analysis of the dominant component of the citrus peel oil, i.e. D-
limonene in the substrate and eluent was conducted using gas chro-
matography (GC) coupled to a mass spectroscopy detector (GC-MS
Trace GC Ultra, ThemoScientiﬁc, Waltham, MA, USA). The GC-MS was
equipped with a silica capillary column (ZB-5MS fused-silica with
30 m × 0.25 mm id × 0.25 μm ﬁlm). Helium was used as the carrier
gas with a ﬂow rate of 1.2 mL/min. The temperature of the column was
set at 50 °C for 2 min, and the temperature was increased to 120 °C with
a rate of 4 °C/min. The injector temperature was set at 250 °C, and the
detector temperature was set at 280 °C. Before analysis, the citrus es-
sential oil was extracted from the sample by diluting 3 g of the sample
with 10 mL of diethyl-ether and shaking overnight at 200 rpm.
The total volume of gas produced from 2 L CSTR (continuous stirred
tank reactor) was measured by the tipping device in the Automatic
Methane Potential Testing System (AMPTS, Bioprocess control AB,
Lund, Sweden). The gas production, yield, and composition were de-
termined based on a measurement using Gas Chromatography (Varian
450 GC, Palo Alto, CA, USA). A gas sample (100 μL) was withdrawn
using a 250 μL gas-tight syringe equipped with a pressure lock (VICI,
Baton Rouge, LA, USA). It was then injected and analyzed with the
Varian 450 Gas Chromatography. The GC was equipped with a Wall
Coated Open Tubular (WCOT, J & W Scientiﬁc GS-Gas Pro, bonded
silica-based 30 m × 0.32 mm, Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA,
USA) capillary column, a thermal conductivity detector (TCD, Varian,
Palo Alto, CA, USA) and Galaxie Chromatography Data System Single
Instrument as the data recording software (v.1.9, Varian, Walnut Creek,
CA, USA). Nitrogen was chosen as the carrier gas with ﬂow rates of
2.0 mL/min passing the column and of 30 mL/min passing the detector.
An injection split ratio was set at 5 with an injector temperature of
75 °C. Meanwhile, the oven, detector heater, and detector ﬁlament
temperatures were set at 55, 120, and 200 °C, respectively. To ascertain
peak retention time and calculate gas production, pure methane (CH4),
carbon dioxide (CO2), and hydrogen (H2) were used as the standard.
The calculation was later done by comparing the peak area of the
sample and the peak area of the standard, followed by conversion to the
steady-state condition (273 K).
2.6. Experimental design and statistical analysis
A two-level three-factor full-factorial experiment design (2k) was
carried out to investigate the eﬀects of ISR, initial O2 presence, BES, and
the interaction between eﬀects towards VFA yield and methane pro-
duction in the ﬁrst culture (for culture eﬀect of ISR, BES, and O2).
Meanwhile, the general multilevel full factorial design was carried out
to investigate the eﬀects of pH, ISR, and the interactions between two
factors towards VFA yield and methane production (for culture eﬀect of
ISR and pH). The experimental design for each culture is presented in
Tables 2 and 3. All experimental setups were carried out in duplicates.
In order to evaluate the inﬂuence of those factors, an analysis of
variance (ANOVA) for the general multilevel factorial design was per-
formed. The means of the signiﬁcantly diﬀerent main eﬀects were
compared at p < 0.05. The statistical analysis was performed using
Minitab 19.

3. Results and discussions
Citrus waste, as a by-product of juice production, is a challenge for
the environment. Its moisture content is too high to be a good feedstock
for combustion and energy production. The presence of toxic com-
pounds from peel oils such as D-limonene also makes it unattractive for
composting and the biogas industries. Methanogens in anaerobic di-
gestion (AD) are the most sensitive groups of the microorganisms.
Hence, there is a possibility to stop the AD process before the metha-
nogens and to produce VFAs instead. However, the question is if one
can obtain a suitable yield of VFAs from citrus wastes. Therefore, in this
work, the eﬀects of diﬀerent digestion conditions with no pH control
during anaerobic digestion of citrus waste were investigated, and four
response parameters, i.e., the yield of VFAs, the amount of biogas, the
pH, and the oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) were studied. The
most important results are summarized in Fig. 2. Based on the results of
this ﬁrst cultivations, in the second experimental setup, the eﬀects of
just ISR together with the eﬀects of diﬀerent controlled pH values were
investigated by following up the same response parameters as within
the ﬁrst cultivations, and the results are summarized in Fig. 4.
3.1. Eﬀect of initial O2 presence, the addition of inhibitor for methanogens,
and ISR on the production of VFAs
The conventional anaerobic digestion process can be shifted to
produce VFAs instead of methane by stopping the degradation at the
acidiﬁcation stage. The conditions should be modiﬁed to be unsuitable
for the VFA consumer, which is methanogens (Wainaina et al., 2019). In
order to inhibit methanogens, several diﬀerent approaches can be
considered such as adding a chemical inhibitor, such as 2-bromoetha-
nesulphonate (BES) (Zinder et al., 1984), or letting O2 be present in the
reactor (Wainaina et al., 2019), along with increasing the substrate
loading (Wainaina et al., 2019). Citrus waste itself has been known to
have an inhibitory eﬀect on methane production in a biogas reactor
(Fuertes, 2015; Kurniawan et al., 2018; Ruiz and Flotats, 2016; Ruiz
Fuertes, 2015; Wikandari, 2014; Wikandari et al., 2015; Wikandari
et al., 2014b). In this ﬁrst cultivation, the eﬀects of inoculum to
substrate ratio (ISR), the addition of BES, and the presence of initial O2
on the yield of VFAs obtained through batch digestion cultivations were
determined and the results are presented in Fig. 1. All of these culti-
vations were carried out at an initial pH of 6, and then the pH remained
uncontrolled during an incubation period of 14 days.
The change of pH values for 14 days for diﬀerent inoculum-sub-
strate ratios, BES, and oxygen conditions with initial pH 6 are shown in
Fig. 1(a). In cases where the ratio of the inoculum-substrate is 1:1, the
pH value has fallen below ﬁve on the second day, and on the 14th day,
it has reached about 4.5 (Fig. 1(a)). On the other hand, when the ratio
of the inoculum-substrate was 1:3, the pH value did not fall below ﬁve
on the second day and decreased below 4.5 on the 14th day (Fig. 1(a)).
In addition, in every case at initial pH 6, a sudden fall of pH occurred
due to the production of VFAs on the second day and then continued
with a closed curve. Cysneiros et al. (2012) showed in their study that
pH dropped on the ﬁrst day and then increased slightly and tended to
stabilize at a particular value. Shahbaz et al. (2019) reported that the
increase of VFA production caused the pH to decrease. In our study, the
same inoculum-substrate ratios, presence or absence of BES and O2 did
not signiﬁcantly aﬀect the pH value.
ORP is an indicator of the net outcome of intracellular metabolism
dominated by electron transfer and redox balance (Liu et al., 2013). The
change of ORP (Oxidation-Reduction Potential) values for 14 days for
diﬀerent inoculum-substrate ratios, BES, and oxygen conditions are
shown in Fig. 1(b). While ORP values were similar for all conditions at
the beginning, ORP values were below 100 when the ratio of the in-
oculum to the substrate was 1:1 on the 14th day, but it was more than
130 on the 14th day in the case of 1:3. In both cases, the ORP values
increased, but all ORP values tend to be stable even if there are minor
changes from the 8th day.
In this cultivation, two diﬀerent inoculum/substrate ratios have
been studied to be 1:1 and 1:3 in order to investigate how VFA pro-
duction is aﬀected when the amount of substrate is increased. As shown
in Fig. 2(a–h). When the amount of substrate is increased, the yield of
VFAs decreased. While the substrate to the inoculum ratio was 1:1, the
amount of acetate and butyrate increased almost the same until the
14th day. When the substrate to inoculum ratio increased (from 1:1 to
1:3), the amount of acetate increased more than the amount of buty-
rate. Similar results were obtained in the study by Xu et al. (2012), BES
was added to prevent VFA consumption by inhibiting the methano-
genesis under anaerobic conditions. Fig. 2 indicates both in the pre-
sence and absence of BES, the proﬁle of the concentration of total VFA,
as well as the individual VFA, including acetic acid, propionic acid,
isobutyric acid, butyric acid, isovaleric acid, valeric acid, and caproic
acid at pH 6. BES is a methanogen inhibitor. Since the addition of BES
in anaerobic conditions prevents methanogen production, VFA pro-
duction is possible. However, as it is observed in Fig. 2(a, b, e, f with
BES vs. c, d, g, h with no BES), the addition of the BES did not make

signiﬁcant changes in the amount of VFA.
In order to investigate the eﬀect of fully anaerobic conditions
(without O2 presence) on VFA production, the headspace was ﬂushed
with a mixture of % 20 CO2 and% 80 N2. The initial presence of oxygen
did not have a signiﬁcant eﬀect (Fig. 2 a, c, e, g vs. b, d, f, h) on the VFA
yield. This fact can be beneﬁcial in the application on a larger scale.
Unlike a methane-based anaerobic digester, this VFA-based reactor is
not as sensitive to oxygen. Since this study was performed under
anaerobic conditions and the last product of the anaerobic digestion is
normally biogas, the gas formation was evaluated in this study. The
biogas production and composition for 14 days for diﬀerent inoculum-
substrate ratios, BES, and oxygen conditions are shown in Fig. 2(i–p).
When comparing Fig. 4(e) and (g), CH4 and CO2 contents appear to be
higher in the non-BES reactor (Fig. 4(g)). Compared to Fig. 4(a) and (c),
hydrogen production, an intermediate product in anaerobic processes
such as VFA, appears to be higher in the BES-containing reactor A
(Fig. 4(a)). In comparison with Fig. 4(a) and (b), oxygen did not have a
signiﬁcant impact on biogas production.
Among the three factors examined in this culture, inoculum to
substrate ratio has been shown to have a signiﬁcant impact on VFA
yield. Higher substrate loading causes a decrease in VFA yield. Not only
aﬀecting methanogens, citrus peel oil containing in the citrus waste,
which predominantly consists of D-Limonene, might also inhibit the
acidiﬁcation of VFAs (Kurniawan et al., 2018; Lukitawesa et al., 2018).
The presence of initial O2 and the addition of inhibitor for methanogens
mostly aﬀect biogas production and do not signiﬁcantly aﬀect the VFA
yield. Since the presence of O2 did not negatively aﬀect the VFA pro-
duction, an acidiﬁcation reactor which is treating citrus waste may not
have to be as strictly anaerobic as a methane production reactor. This
fact can simplify the maintenance of the reactor, during which it
sometimes needs to be opened.
3.2. Eﬀect of diﬀerent controlled pH on VFA production
In the second culture, the eﬀect of pH control was investigated to-
gether with the inoculum substrate ratio. Four parameters were ob-
served, i.e., volatile fatty acid (VFA) production and volatile fatty acid
(VFA) yield, gas production, pH, and ORP. The cultivations were car-
ried out by increasing pH (4, 5 and 6) and inoculum substrate ratio (1:1,
1:3). Since pH and ORP are essential parameters for system stabilization
in biological systems, pH and ORP values have been recorded in this
culture for 22 days.
In this cultivation, the pH at three diﬀerent pH values was con-
trolled during 22 days, where the pH was adjusted back to the starting
pH every second days. The change of pH values for diﬀerent inoculum-
substrate ratios and diﬀerent pH controlled or uncontrolled were
measured during the experiment. In all conditions (Fig. 5(a) and (b)),
pH values showed signiﬁcant changes during the ﬁrst six days. How-
ever, from the 8th day onwards, the changes were more stable and
closer to the constant level. Moreover, in general, a sudden fall occurred
due to the production of VFAs on the second day and then continued
with a closed curve. Similarly, Kim et al. (2003) found that at the be-
ginning of the acidiﬁcation of food waste, the pH dropped steeply and
stabilized afterward.
The change of ORP values for diﬀerent inoculum-substrate ratios
and diﬀerent pH values is presented in Fig. 3(b). The ORP values for all
conditions were ﬂuctuated during the ﬁrst eight days. After the 8th day,
the ORP become more stable. ORP decreased, and VFA accumulated
slowed after day 8. A similar trend was previously reported by Yin et al.
(2016). When the inoculum-substrate ratios were 1:1 and 1:3, and the
pH was 4, the ORP value was around 190 at the end of the 2 s day,
while at pH 5 it was about 125 and pH 6 it was about 70.
In order to determine the eﬀect of pH change on the production of
VFAs in this culture, three diﬀerent pH values (4, 5, and 6) were ex-
amined. An extremely acidic (less than 3) or extremely alkaline pH
(more than 12) can inhibit the acidogens (Wainaina et al., 2019).
Therefore, this study was carried out with three diﬀerent pH values of
4, 5 and 6. VFA yield tended to decrease when pH was increased
(Fig. 4(a–f) and Table 5). In both cases (1:1 and 1:3), the highest VFA
production and yield were at pH 6. Jiang et al. (2013) reported also a
similar study with three diﬀerent pH values (5, 6 and 7) and reached
the highest VFA production at pH 6. At pH 4, while one of the dominant
species was propionate, the propionate value decreased as the pH gets
higher, and it was undetectable. When the pH increased, acetate and
butyrate yields increased, as observed in Fig. 4(a and c), while no
caproate value was present at pH 4. Caproate was produced at pH 5 and
6, as shown in Fig. 4(b, c, e, and f).
In this second culture, it was investigated how the ratio of inoculum
substrate with diﬀerent pH values aﬀects the production of VFAs. The
VFA yield decreased as the ratio of inoculum substrate changed from
1:1 to 1:3 (Table 4). Since this study was performed under anaerobic
conditions and the last product of the anaerobic digestion was biogas.
Gas measurements were made in this study. The biogas production and
composition for 22 days for diﬀerent inoculum-substrate ratios and
diﬀerent pH values are shown in Fig. 4(g–l). The incubation time was
only 22 days because, in our preliminary study, there was no increase in
VFA production afterward (data not shown). Studies by Zhou et al.
(2016) showed that the performance of anaerobic digestion was
strongly dependent on pH value. They worked with three diﬀerent pH
and achieved the highest amount of biogas 16.6 mL at pH 7.
The biogas yield increased as the pH increased (Fig. 4(i–k)). When
pH was constant, and the biogas production decreased as the inoculum-
substrate ratio increased. In addition, biogas production decreased as
pH increased compared to Fig. 4(l–n).

eventually hinders the microbial productivity (van der Wielen et al.,

4. Conclusions
Citrus waste can be converted into VFAs through controlled anae-
robic digestion at low substrate loading. The most signiﬁcant factor in
this study is inoculum to substrate ratio and controlling pH. The highest
yield of VFAs of 0.793 g VFA/VS was achieved by controlling the pH at
6 and low substrate loading (ISR 1:1) with the presence of initial O2.
Higher substrate loading resulted in the VFA yield to decrease. In
practical application, controlling the pH is most likely the most im-
portant factor determining VFA yield. Besides, as oxygen does not have
a signiﬁcant eﬀect on VFA yield, the presence of small amount of
oxygen or opening the reactor for maintenance does not harm the
digestion process.
